triage.modern_statement: This is not a single question that can be stated precisely. The note is a reading or study list headed 'Realitätsfragen' ('questions of reality'). In 19th-century German algebra and geometry, this phrase meant questions about real versus complex solutions. Examples are how many real roots a system has, how many real inflection points or bitangents a curve has, and how many real components a real algebraic curve or surface has and where they lie. The names fit this reading. Kronecker counted real roots using the Kronecker characteristic or index. Dyck generalized Kronecker's characteristic in his 'Beiträge zur Analysis situs'. Klein studied the real shape of plane curves, including Klein's formula relating real singularities. Franz Meyer wrote on apolarity and rational curves, including their real properties. In modern terms the note points at real algebraic geometry: counting real solutions, and the topology of the real points of real algebraic varieties. It names an area to study, not a specific statement to prove.
triage.answered_by: There is no single answer. The theme continued in Hilbert's own work and became part of his 16th problem (1900), which asks about the topology of real algebraic curves and surfaces. Rokhlin, Gudkov, Viro and others made major progress on that problem in the 20th century. It is still open in general.
